regions.text: 光實せる具證約全體である限り單なる必然者でもなく單なる偶然者でもなく、必然と偶然との相開に於て意味を有する「必然し偶然者」である。

quote.translation: The absolute, in short, insofar as it is not an empty abstract whole but a fulfilled concrete whole, is neither the merely necessary nor the merely contingent: it is the necessary-contingent, which has its meaning in the correlation of the necessary and the contingent.

regions.text: さうして絶對者は相對なる有限者によつて初めて絶對者たり得るもの、換言すれば偶然分として他在することによつて初めて絶對的全置の具體的意味を獲得するものであるから、「必然1偶然者としての絶對者は絶對者の舞歴法に於ける即、自且對自の毀階と考へても差支ないであらう。

quote.translation: And since the absolute can be the absolute only through the relative, finite thing, which is to say that it acquires the concrete meaning of the absolute whole only by existing as other in contingent parts, there will be no harm in thinking the absolute as the necessary-contingent as the stage of the in-and-for-itself in the dialectic of the absolute.

regions.text: なほまた、原始偶然が因果系列の各成員を部分とする全體と考へ得る限り、原始偶然と經驗必然との翻係に死ても、形而上的必然と形而上偶然との開係に開してと全く同様な考察をすることが出來るのは云ふまでもない。

quote.translation: It goes without saying, moreover, that insofar as primal contingency can be thought as the whole that has each member of the causal series as its parts, exactly the same consideration can be made of the relation between primal contingency and empirical necessity as of the relation between metaphysical necessity and metaphysical contingency.

regions.text: 以上に於て原始偶然と絶對形而上約必然とが「必然ー偶然者」としての絶對者の雨面であることを明かになし得たと信ずる。

quote.translation: I believe I have now made clear that primal contingency and absolute metaphysical necessity are two sides of the absolute as the necessary-contingent.

regions.text: 次に、經驗必然と形而上偶然との開係は如何。

quote.translation: What, next, is the relation between empirical necessity and metaphysical contingency?

regions.text: 假説的地平に於ける経驗必然が離接的地平に於ては形而上約偶然となつて現はれる。

quote.translation: Empirical necessity on the hypothetical horizon appears on the disjunctive horizon as metaphysical contingency.

regions.text: ライプニッツは形而上學敍說」のうちで必然（niccssaire）と確質（Certain）との區別を立てようとして

quote.translation: Leibniz, in the Discourse on Metaphysics, seeking to set up a distinction between the necessary (nécessaire) and the certain (certain), holds that the former is that whose opposite contains a contradiction and the latter that whose opposite does not, and that since only the absolutely necessary (absolument nécessaire) is necessary in the strict sense, the hypothetically necessary (nécessaire ex hypothesi) is no more than certain.
